item.title: The (human) emotional part of doing maths
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: "All the relationships are emotional," shouted a stranger on the street. Turns out that's true even for mathematics. Emotion may be one of the most human things we have. Judging by what AI still can't do, perhaps we should cherish this irrational part more.
item.content:encoded:
A follow-up to Shmuel Weinberger’s post

Luise Ge, PhD student in computer science at Washington University St Louis

First, the not so serious part: emotions

Someone was shouting in her vernacular accent: “Because all the relationships are emotional!” just now, at 11pm.

It was so loud that I heard it as clearly as possible from the fifth floor.

It broke my concentration and made my mind switch to something different: maybe instead of saying I am a mathematician which actually made me feel nervous because i am no longer in a math department, I should say I am someone that have a deep relationship with it. How do i prove it? Because I have had and plan to continue having so many strong emotions with it!

Here is a list:

Euphoria: When I proved something successfully, blimey, I am the happiest person in the world.

Empowered: I am so grateful that I can understand a lot of physics, biology, chemistry, computer science or music because I know maths.

Humbled: Why are large number so large? Why are we still knowing so little about everything?

Dread: I was not good at maths during high school, and maths exams at that time gave me tremendous nerves. I think it was to the level of panic attacks.

Sublimity: To me the Euler equation is like a Flemish painting I could hang on my wall; the aesthetic experience of an elegant is as haughty as listening to Bach’s music, but a little bit scary when thinking about higher dimensional space and topology (see, for example, this video).

Anticipation: When I was going to learn a new topic, I would feel super excited.

Repose: I remember, for example, going over lecture notes for revision, and seeing all the definitions and theorems and lemmas connecting with each other makes me feel extremely organized and calm.

Camaraderie: The quarrels between you and your teammate can get so intense and heated that outsiders wouldn’t understand, but when the problem’s solved, we are the best teammates together.

Isolation: I felt sour when all my friends went out on Friday night.

Desolation: Does the never-ending tunnel resonates with you?

Tenacity: Is it about faith in myself, faith in the conjecture, or just because there is no exit?

Grounding: As I am doing CS, formal verification of things and some provable bounds give me something i can grip on and feel grounded by.

Bewilderment: Just dazed and confused.

Second, are they really not so serious?—\text{\textemdash}or, what are emotions good for?

I travelled to an AI conference recently focused on integrating reasoning and learning; one of the main goals of this community (check inductive logic programming, for instance) is automated discovery, defining new entities and finding relationships between them, from atoms to genes. This is not a new dream either. As brought up by keynote speaker Prof. Stephen Muggleton, Turing1 once pondered a question about whether a machine can generate new ideas like a nuclear chain reaction.

Discovery to me is the most exciting, and grandiose objective of AI, as it has truly propelled the development of our civilization.

As for mathematical creation, it feels like these mysterious emotions, like the sense of “rightness”, or surprise, curiosity are like the little fairies guiding us to the destinations.

And this is the part current AI has not be able to do yet.

Maybe partially it’s because AI doesn’t have emotions yet but we do?

Maybe our human emotions will still make us better mathematicians, sometimes, and for a while?

Maybe we should try to always keep it this way?

And be wary that when we work with AI, our feelings seem to be less deep, and less varied.

Received 24 September 2026.

  1. The passage (responding to Lady Lovelace’s objection that a machine can only do what it’s told) reads: a person can “inject” an idea into a mind or machine, and it will respond to some extent and then die away —\text{\textemdash} like a piano string struck by a hammer. Turing then extends the simile to an atomic pile below critical size: an injected idea corresponds to a neutron entering the pile from outside, causing a disturbance that eventually dies away —\text{\textemdash} unless the pile is large enough, in which case the disturbance keeps growing until the whole pile goes up.
    He then applies this directly to minds: most human minds seem to be “sub-critical,” meaning an idea presented to them gives rise, on average, to less than one idea in reply, while a smaller proportion are “supercritical,” where an idea can set off a whole cascade of secondary and tertiary ideas. He notes animal minds seem clearly sub-critical, and then poses the question your talk seems to have been built around: can a machine be made to be super-critical? ︎

item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “As many of you, I feel lost in the new world. I am gaining experience and face questions I find hard to answer and choices I find hard to make. For this reason, I wanted to create a very minimal set of axioms which I can quickly apply when I am not sure. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Jarek Kędra, Professor at University of Aberdeen

As many of you, I feel lost in the new world. I am gaining experience and face questions I find hard to answer and choices I find hard to make. For this reason, I wanted to create a very minimal set of axioms which I can quickly apply when I am not sure. Also, I wanted them to be helpful in discussions about the new shape of mathematical research and education. They are not original very likely obvious to many of you, and they go back to Thurston, at least. I wrote them mainly for my personal use. Here is version 1.0.

AXIOMS v.1.0

  1. Mathematics is done to deepen human understanding.
  2. Mathematics advances only through human understanding.
  3. Independent human mathematical thought must be preserved.

item.title: Mathematics Year Zero
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: It was the image of a bombardment that came to my mind on the day OpenAI announced the resolution of 372 major problems in mathematics: destroyed theses, shattered academic lives, research fields in ruins, and the evidence of a brutal shift of era in which a company asserts its superpower without regard for those it has just crushed.
item.content:encoded:
Charles Bordenave, CNRS research director at Aix-Marseille University

AI use: I did not use generative AI to write this text (apart grammar/ proof checking). It was originally written in French and it was translated with the help of QWEN3.8, an open weight model.

It was the image of a bombardment that came to my mind on the day OpenAI announced the resolution of 372 major problems in mathematics across 719 manuscripts: destroyed theses, shattered academic lives, research fields in ruins, and the evidence of a brutal shift of era in which a company asserts its superpower without regard for those it has just crushed.

I am not in the habit of giving my opinion publicly on my discipline. I trust collective deliberations more, which carry far more weight and legitimacy. But reading the very numerous high-quality contributions on this site, I wanted to add my small stone to this collective work of mourning our past life, of which this site is becoming, day by day, the place.

Why be so dramatic? The young people who embrace the demanding path of mathematics are our most precious collective asset. They may be the first victims of the revolution underway. A decline in positions is to be feared as early as 2027 in North American universities, and it could spread throughout the world. Students risk turning away from mathematics. Without even speaking of uncertainties in the job market, the symbolic and romantic force of our discipline has collapsed, and without it, we will no longer attract young people seeking understanding and universalism.

Obviously, the production of new knowledge in mathematics has exploded and one can only marvel at the truly superhuman feats accomplished by generative AIs. I will not dwell on the reasons pushing OpenAI, Anthropic and others toward this trophy race to theorems, we are but collateral victims of stakes that far exceed our community. Even when these companies turn away from mathematics, the AI revolution in our discipline will continue its development. It might perhaps even open up desirable horizons. But for that, we must organize ourselves to collectively survive this change of era.

Here are some proposals:

  • Let us preserve the unity of our community and keep dialogue open between our different opinions and strategies in the face of this revolution. The transparency on AI tools and models used, if any, should be the norm in our works.
  • Let us stop using OpenAI tools to conduct research and let us write in our articles “We did not use for this project generative AI provided by OpenAI, whose practices do not meet the standards of our community”. As highlighted by the Association for Human Mathematics, this company is out of step with the ethics of our profession and has shown us nothing but contempt, even in the face of our dialogue initiatives such as that of the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, or as illustrated by the testimony of Tristan Buckmaster. Its practices are opaque and take advantage of our completely open academic world. I know of no real necessity for such an acceleration of mathematical research to meet the needs of other sciences or of society. Let us take the time to digest what has been produced in a few months.

Beyond the case of OpenAI, we should demand of all concerned companies that they accept the most elementary ethical recommendations, such as those formulated in the Leiden Declaration or by the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence. In a few years, we could have an open-source generative AI model controlled by the academic world. With such a model, we will have control over the financial and ecological costs we are willing to bear to advance our discipline, and we will be able to protect ourselves against a multi-speed discipline, depending on the wealth of universities and their proximity to AI companies.

  • Let us fight to preserve positions, at least initially. We have trained young mathematicians: it is our duty to help them find employment, security and guarantee fair conditions of access to these jobs regardless of their use of generative AIs.
  • Let us redefine the contours of our discipline and our profession. New fields and practices of mathematics will emerge, interdisciplinary research will develop, public outreach and mathematical culture could enter a golden age, mathematics becoming so accessible. This could prevent the foreseeable decline in the number of mathematics students.
  • Let us invest in the field of AI safety. We are experiencing this directly: AI raises very numerous critical challenges for our societies, such as cybersecurity and financial security, or the risk of cognitive collapse. Mathematics can contribute to this emerging field. We cannot leave it to the companies developing AI to decide what is the proper use of AI for tomorrow’s society.
  • Let us defend a right to non-use of AI in all professional tasks, in all professions, in the same way that we have a right to digital disconnection.

The title of this text refers to Germany Year Zero, a masterpiece by Roberto Rossellini. It follows a child, alone in a Berlin in ruins, who brings to mind our young mathematicians. I hope that we will know how to avoid a tragedy.

Received 12 October 2026.

item.title: Why and how to transparently disclose AI use in mathematics research
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: With the goal of standardising AI disclosures, I argue for the inclusion of maximally transparent AI disclosures in mathematics research. I provide concrete and actionable guiding principles, a taxonomy and a LaTeX package for implementation.
item.content:encoded:
Maximilian Kaipel, postdoc at Bielefeld University

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

This is a summary of an article written by me with the same title. This summary is presented without references for the sake of brevity. The full version of this article can be found on my personal website.

In August 2026, almost 25% of all mathematics articles uploaded to arXiv disclosed the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies. Among these, one finds varying levels of detail describing the human-AI-interaction and its impact on the article. Unsurprisingly, one study has found a significant discrepancy between expectations and the reality of AI disclosures in computer science, and many mathematicians likely share this feeling. For this reason, I want to initiate a standardisation of AI disclosures in mathematics. With this goal in mind, I surveyed existing guidelines, recommendations and the work of scholars on research ethics. The outcome of my endeavours is the development of three guiding principles, a taxonomy and a LaTeX package.

Why transparent disclosure is important

Commercial Large Language Models (LLMs) pose many ethical concerns for society and science in general, and for mathematics in particular. While detection tools for AI-generated text remain unreliable, a complete ban on the use of such technologies for mathematics is infeasible. Instead, I argue that academic journals, which are likely to experience a significant increase in submissions, should require maximally transparent AI disclosures going forward. In addition, many existing structures in academia fundamentally depend on the correct attribution of ideas. While it is possible to challenge the status quo, I assume here that it is desirable to uphold this tradition. Even without this assumption, transparent AI use disclosure is beneficial for approximating expended financial and environmental resources, thus providing insight into the sustainability of AI-assisted mathematics. Indeed, “transparency” and “reproducibility” are listed among the most important guiding principles of the UNESCO Recommendations on Open Science. These axioms of responsible research demand a maximally transparent AI disclosure. In fact, under current policies, it is considered academic misconduct to omit disclosure of AI tool use for mathematics research.

The guiding principles

In its simplest form, the human-AI-interaction discussed here may be described as a cycle

Human provides AI input -> AI produces output -> Human processes AI output -> Human provides AI input

which eventually terminates in the production of a mathematics research article. A transparent AI disclosure allows readers to correctly identify the role played by AI technologies throughout the entire process of creating the research manuscript.

Who should be author?

Many others have discussed the question of who should be the author on a (mathematics) research manuscript to which AI contributed. Authorship is primarily an indicator of credit for the progress made in the research article and most scholars on research ethics agree that credit and responsibility are two sides of the same coin. This implies that in order to receive credit, one must assume responsibility. However, as AI tools are not human they cannot be held responsible and may therefore not be authors of (mathematics) research manuscripts.

Principle 1: Only humans are able to assume responsibility for the quality of mathematics research and may therefore assume authorship of a research article in mathematics.

How specific should the disclosure be?

With the goal of achieving a maximally transparent AI disclosure, one must necessarily be as specific as possible. Here, I distinguish between three types of specificity: technological, functional and locational. Technological specificity demands the exact description of the AI tool’s name and any additional attributes used, for example GPT-5.6 Sol with max reasoning. Functional specificity is supposed to describe precisely which tasks of the research process were delegated to AI technologies. I developed the Mathematics AI Delegation Taxonomy (MAIDeT), see below, which is designed to provide a standardised dictionary for this purpose. For example, authors may delegate “Statement generation” or “Novelty assessment” to AI and should disclose this clearly. For locational specificity, consider a mathematics article as consisting of three levels: Indexed environments such as lemmas, definitions or theorems; sections; and the entirety of the manuscript. Locational specificity requires the authors to describe as precisely as possible where, for example in Lemma 3.5, in the manuscript a task was delegated to AI.

Principle 2: AI disclosure should be of the highest possible technological, functional and locational specificity.

Why should AI interactions be documented?

Even with the researchers’ input prompts available, readers are not able to reproduce any reported interactions with AI tools. This makes it of utmost importance to document the entirety of the human-AI-interaction for the sake of transparency and reproducibility. Depending on the technology used, this can be as easy as exporting a chat log as a PDF. The inclusion of this documentation can provide insight into token costs and help illuminate the question of sustainability of AI-assisted mathematics.

Principle 3: Every interaction with AI which has influenced the final presentation or content of a manuscript should be recorded in full and made available.

Visibility of AI-critical positions

Commercially available LLMs raise many ethical concerns both generally as well as for mathematics specifically. Together with the issues of transparency and reproducibility, these issues compile an excessive list of reasons for mathematicians to boycott the use of such technologies. For those holding this stance, I strongly recommend including in their research outputs a statement sharing their conviction, which enhances the visibility of AI-critical positions.

Taxonomy and LaTeX package

In order to implement Principle 2 in practice, I developed MAIDeT and a LaTeX package called mathaidisclose. The taxonomy draws on my own experience as a researcher in abstract algebra and many accounts of “doing mathematics” before and after the advent of LLMs. It breaks up five major themes, representing the non-linear research process of doing mathematics, into minor research tasks one may delegate to AI tools. It is important to emphasise that many mathematicians do not view mathematics as a theorem-production pipeline. While some support the philosophy of theorem-proving-above-all-else, viewing it as the one true way of doing mathematics is a serious misrepresentation of mathematics. The taxonomy can be found below:

Knowledge acquisition: 

  • Axiomatisation
  • Example generation
  • Literature search
  • Pattern observation

Objective identification:

  • Applicability assessment
  • Conjecture generation
  • Feasibility assessment
  • Idea generation
  • Novelty assessment
  • Objective formulation
  • Objective subdivision
  • Research gap identification

Proof construction:

  • Statement generation
  • Proof completion
  • Proof generation
  • Proof verification
  • Proof polishing

Code and computation:

  • Algorithm conceptualisation
  • Algorithm implementation
  • Code generation
  • Code optimisation
  • Computation
  • Computation verification
  • Enumeration
  • Formal verification
  • Process automation

Presentation and communication:

  • Context discussion
  • Literature review
  • Proof exposition
  • Reformatting
  • Spell-checking
  • Text generation
  • Translation
  • Trend identification
  • Visualisation

The LaTeX package mathaidisclose allows users to easily implement locational specificity. For example using the command \discloseAI[model]{task} inside of an indexed environment, such as Definition 3.1, will print the sentence: “The authors disclose the delegation of task to model in Definition 3.1” in the AI disclosure section generated using \printAIdisclosure[]. A similar command \globalAIuse[model]{task} is available to disclose the tasks delegated to AI throughout the entirety of the manuscript. For those disclosures which do not fit into the previous ways of disclosing AI use, the command \customAIdisclosure{text} can be used to print any text in the AI disclosure section. This command should also be used by authors to affirm that they have verified all AI-generated outputs included in the article for correctness and that they assume full responsibility for the contents of the manuscript. If none of the three commands for disclosing AI are used, then \printAIdisclosure[] outputs “There is no use of Artificial Intelligence to disclose.”
